codebase-memory-mcp is an MCP server that gives AI agents local code intelligence. It builds a persistent knowledge graph on your machine that connects source code with documentation, configuration, and infrastructure. You can use it to find an unfamiliar feature, follow a call across services, trace a deployment back to its source, or see which parts of a project a change might affect.

Your coding agent gets structural context through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and you can also query the graph directly from the CLI. The MCP server is the core of the project. There is an optional visual companion, CBM Lens, in open beta at v0.0.1, which includes a source reader, architecture maps, the Galaxy graph, coverage diagnostics, architecture decisions, and local code chat.

A native C backend exposes 17 MCP tools, parses languages and file formats with vendored grammars, and provides Hybrid LSP type resolution for supported languages. The installer supports 45 client integrations, some automatic and some conditional, and covers client configuration, skills, agent profiles, and applicable hooks. Indexing and graph queries run locally, with no hosted service or API key. Focused graph queries can reduce repeated file reads and token use; see the measured results.

Your agents can burn 80% fewer tokens. Graphify Cloud gives them always-on memory, governs how they behave, keeps code quality high, and uses formal verification to prove correctness. The free trial runs 14 days.

Inside your AI coding assistant, typing /graphify maps the whole project into a knowledge graph: code, docs, PDFs, images, videos. You query it instead of grepping through files.

How it works:
- Mapping code costs nothing and runs entirely on your machine. Parsing uses tree-sitter AST, which is deterministic and involves no LLM, so nothing leaves your machine. For docs, PDFs, images and video, the semantic pass runs on your assistant's model or a configured API key.
- Every edge comes with an explanation. Connections are tagged EXTRACTED when they are explicit in the source, or INFERRED when graphify resolved them, so you can tell what was read directly from what was worked out.
- This is not a vector index. There are no embeddings and no vector store, just a real graph you can traverse. Ask a question, trace the path between two things, or get one concept explained.

If you want it running all the time, Graphify Cloud keeps the graph live across your entire SDLC. It supports monorepos and cross-repo work, does formal verification, and gives code review a bird's-eye view of your SDLC. Connectors for Sentry, Jira and more put incidents and tickets in the same graph as your code. Start the free 14-day trial at app.graphify.com.

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector for package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers a narrow supply-chain question: when an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines have a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs help answer what shipped, and EDR helps answer what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs a different view, though: messy local state spread across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Given an exposure catalog, it flags exact matches, so responders who already know what they are looking for can run a fast, read-only exposure check.

Autoresearch

Autoresearch turns Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an engine that keeps improving on its own while you're away.

The approach is based on Karpathy's autoresearch. You set a constraint, define a mechanical metric, and let the agent iterate autonomously. The gains compound over time.

The workflow is simple: you set the goal, the agent runs the loop, and you check the results later. You don't need AGI for this. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that keeps running.

The core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification support Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails are available for Claude Code through its native hooks and for pi through extension events.

Fork-and-flush helps metric loops escape plateaus, following the approach described by Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447). At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas, which adds randomness. The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). In Guided mode, R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it responds with FORK before giving up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

CLI Printing Press

Time and money are what nobody wants to waste, and for AI agents that means speed and token spend. When a CLI is designed well, an agent builds muscle memory around it: no digging through docs, no wrong turns, no wasted tokens. That is why we built the Printing Press, a machine for printing CLIs for agents.

It reads the official API docs, studies the popular community CLIs and MCP servers, and sniffs the web for APIs that were never published, like Google Flights or Dominos. It applies the power-user playbook Peter Steinberger proved with discrawl and gogcli: local SQLite, compound commands, agent-native flags. From all of that it prints a token-efficient Go CLI, a Claude Code skill, and an MCP server for any API or any website.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that measures whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across different domains. It is designed to show how much a model's ability to solve complex real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills available.

To test performance in conditions closer to production, where many Skills are installed at once, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original setup, each task comes with only the specialized Skill for that task. In our version, every task runs in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, with all other experimental conditions unchanged. This lets us see whether an agent can find, select, and orchestrate the relevant Skills from a large installed pool and organize them into a workflow that completes the task.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench, using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, while reducing token consumption by 29.6% and tool calls by 33.1%.

sem is a semantic version control tool that works on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, extracts every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at the entity level rather than by lines. So instead of lines x-y changed, you see function blahh was modified.

It works in any Git repo with no setup.

Cloud-backed queries are opt-in per repo. Logging in does not upload a repo or send a query. See the cloud consent flow for the public/private repo states, preview screen, local audit log, and forget controls.

Agentic Context Engine (ACE)

ACE is the open-source engine behind Kayba. If you would rather have the whole loop managed for you, from investigating failures to shipping fixes as PRs, you can get a demo.

AI agents don't learn from experience. They repeat the same mistakes in every session, forget what worked, and ignore what failed. ACE is an open-source engine that adds a persistent learning loop. It also powers Kayba, a managed service that does this for your production agents automatically.

As an example, the agent claims a seahorse emoji exists. ACE reflects on the error, and on the next attempt the agent responds correctly, with no human intervention.
